title: Trade-Winds Environmental Restoration, Inc. v. Stewart — 2008 partial-summary-judgment order
lead: A contractor’s emergency hurricane cleanup led to a multimillion-dollar billing dispute, but Louisiana’s unsuspended licensing laws limited its remaining recovery to actual costs from the building owner.

actors.name: Trade-Winds Environmental Restoration
actors.role: Contractor hired for mold remediation at Heritage Plaza.

actors.name: Stirling Properties
actors.role: Leasing manager and disclosed agent for Stewart Development.

proceedings: Trade-Winds sued June 27, 2006; Judge Ivan L. R. Lemelle granted defendants’ partial-summary-judgment motion in the order signed January 24 and filed January 28, 2008.
limits: This order did not determine the remaining unjust-enrichment amount, order repayment of sums already paid, or decide later insurance proceedings or the 2011 appeal. It applies Louisiana law at the time.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Katrina damage produces an urgent contract
paragraphs: Hurricane Katrina left Heritage Plaza in Metairie with water damage and a significant mold problem. Stewart Development owned the building; Stirling Properties managed leasing and acted as its agent; Travelers Indemnity Company of Connecticut insured it. Trade-Winds Environmental Restoration contacted Stirling employee David Kopp about remediation. Stirling and Trade-Winds signed a September 22, 2005 agreement with an open-ended time-and-materials price based on Trade-Winds’ rate sheet.

Trade-Winds then held neither a Louisiana general-contractor license nor a mold-remediation license. It applied for the latter on September 28 and received it on February 16, 2006. Trade-Winds alleged that it completed the work on March 11, after the license issued. The eventual contract dispute nevertheless turned on its unlicensed status when the agreement was made.

sections.title: The unpaid bill brings the parties into court
paragraphs: Defendants alleged that Trade-Winds originally estimated a $750,000 job but ultimately billed more than $9 million through questionable billing practices. They said they repeatedly sought supporting documentation, paid $7.5 million, and refused further payment when the documentation did not arrive. These were allegations, not findings of billing fraud or findings that every disputed charge was improper.

Trade-Winds sued on June 27, 2006 for the asserted unpaid balance. On December 11, 2007 the defendants moved for partial summary judgment. Stewart Development argued that the unlicensed contract was invalid. Stirling invoked its status as a disclosed agent, while Trade-Winds argued that knowingly hiring an unlicensed contractor exceeded the agent’s authority. Travelers denied that Trade-Winds was insured or had a claim under its policy. Trade-Winds responded with allegations of an insurance-payment scheme and a possible third-party benefit in an indemnification agreement.

sections.title: An enforcement pause had not suspended the licensing laws
paragraphs: The applicable Louisiana statutes required an active contractor license for covered commercial construction or repair costing at least $50,000, and a separate license for mold remediation, including removal, cleaning, sanitizing, demolition, and treatment of contaminated matter. Trade-Winds did not dispute that its work fell within these definitions or that it lacked both licenses at formation. Louisiana decisions treated such contracts as null and void, while permitting unjust enrichment for actual materials, services, and labor costs.

Trade-Winds offered an affidavit from Charles Marceaux, executive director of the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors. After Katrina, the Board had delayed aggressive enforcement for ninety days, September 1 through December 1, 2005. It continued publicizing the requirements and retained authority to act against contractors detrimental to the public, although it had not acted against Trade-Winds. Governors had suspended debris-removal licensing rules after other hurricanes, but Governor Blanco had issued no comparable suspension after Katrina.

Two earlier Trade-Winds cases had approached this issue differently. Biomedical Applications denied summary judgment because questions remained about suspension and the informal policy’s legal effect. St. Tammany Park held that relaxed enforcement did not remove the prohibition. Here the parties agreed on the policy’s existence and disputed its legal effect, leaving a question the court could resolve on summary judgment.

sections.title: The court refuses to enforce the bargain but preserves actual costs
paragraphs: Judge Ivan L. R. Lemelle distinguished administrative enforcement discretion from statutory suspension. Choosing not to enforce aggressively did not repeal or suspend the legal requirements for a valid contract. Trade-Winds’ September 22 agreement was therefore null and void.

Trade-Winds argued that this result would discourage specialists from helping after disasters. The court answered that Louisiana’s legislature had chosen licensing protections against incompetent, inexperienced, unlawful, or fraudulent contracting and against injury or misleading mold-remediation practices. A judge could not substitute a different emergency policy. State law allowed the Governor to suspend certain regulatory statutes during emergencies, but no necessary order had been issued. The Board’s retained selective-enforcement power also contradicted the idea that licensing obligations had disappeared.

Stirling’s alleged knowledge could not estop defendants from invoking those laws. Private acceptance of unlicensed work could not validate a prohibited agreement. This defeated contractual enforcement against Stewart Development while leaving a claim for actual-cost unjust enrichment. It did not make the full invoice recoverable under another name.

sections.title: The agent and insurer obtain separate dismissals
paragraphs: Louisiana Civil Code article 3016 generally protected an agent contracting in its principal’s name within its authority; article 3019 could impose personal liability for exceeding authority, subject to exceptions. Trade-Winds relied on article 3019 and Kopp’s testimony that he knew in late September that a license had been requested but not received. The court reasoned that those provisions concerned execution of a contract, whereas no valid contract existed here. Trade-Winds supplied no authority for recovering from Stirling the invoice amounts, fees, and costs unavailable against its principal. The court dismissed the claims against Stirling in its agency capacity; it did not announce immunity for agents’ independent misconduct.

Against Travelers, Trade-Winds alleged false offsets and a payment-suppression scheme. It knew an indemnification agreement existed but did not know its terms. A stipulation pour autrui—a contract benefit enforceable by a third party—required a manifestly clear benefit and could not be presumed. The mere existence of an indemnification agreement did not establish that benefit or a genuine issue for trial. The Louisiana Attorney General’s allegations against insurers in a different lawsuit likewise supplied no specific evidence of a scheme in this dispute. Travelers obtained dismissal.

The order, signed January 24 and filed January 28, 2008, dismissed the contract claim against Stewart Development and the claims against Stirling and Travelers. Trade-Winds’ remaining claims against Stewart Development were limited to unjust enrichment for actual materials, services, and labor costs. The court fixed no restitution amount, directed no repayment of the $7.5 million already paid, and did not resolve the entire litigation.
